fig:universal.title: Left: the universal property of the product. Every pair of arrows $f$, $g$ out of $X$ factors through one arrow $h=(f,g)$ into $A\times B$. Right: the naturality square of a natural transformation $\eta \colon F\Rightarrow G$. Going right then down equals going down then right

fig:v10new-ch01-divisors.title: The divisors of $12$, ordered by divisibility. Each upward edge is an arrow, and longer arrows are obtained by composition. The greatest common source of $4$ and $6$ is $2$, their product in this category. Their least common target is $12$, their coproduct

fig:v10new-ch01-yoneda.title: Yoneda's determination of a natural transformation. The upper arrow sends $\mathrm {id}_A$ to $f$; the lower arrow sends $x=\alpha _A(\mathrm {id}_A)$ to $F(f)(x)$. Commutativity forces $\alpha _B(f)=F(f)(x)$ for every $f$

cor:yonedaemb.title: an object is known by its maps

linear:ch:tensors.title: Tensors and the Cost of Multiplying Matrices

linear:exa:rotation.title: the rank depends on the field

linear:fig:wtensor.title: The tensor $W$ as a cube of entries. Its front slice $A$ is a permutation matrix and its back slice $B$ has a single $1$; since $A^{-1}B$ is a non-zero nilpotent matrix, $W$ has rank $3$, yet it is a limit of tensors of rank $2$

linear:fig:omega.title: Upper bounds for the exponent $\omega $ of matrix multiplication, from Strassen's $\log _27\approx 2.807$ (1969) to $2.3713$ (2024). Since Coppersmith and Winograd (1990), all progress has come from the same ``laser method'', refined: $2.3755$, then $2.3729$ (2012), $2.37286$ (2014), and, after three smaller steps, $2.37134$ (2024). These bounds are quoted, not proved here. The lower bound is still $\omega \ge 2$

fig:v10new-ch02-vectorization.title: Column vectorisation of a $2\times 3$ matrix. Entries from each column remain together in the vector. This order is why right multiplication by $B$ becomes $B^{\mathsf T}\otimes I$ and left multiplication by $A$ becomes $I\otimes A$

fig:v10new-ch02-recursion.title: Strassen recursion at $n=2^s$. Depth $j$ contains $7^j$ products of blocks of side $n/2^j$. At depth $s$ there are $7^s$ scalar products. The additions made at depth $j<s$ cost $18\cdot 7^j(n/2^{j+1})^2$, which must also be counted

fig:snake.title: The snake lemma. The kernels of the vertical maps sit above the diagram, their cokernels below; the connecting homomorphism $\partial $ is the snake's body, running from the top right to the bottom left. To compute $\partial (z)$: lift $z$ to $y\in B$, push it down to $b(y)\in B'$, which lies in $f'(A')$, pull it back to $x'\in A'$, and take its class

fig:v10new-ch03-collapse.title: Tensoring with $\Z /2$ preserves the quotient at the right but turns the first injection into zero. The lower row is exact at its middle and right non-zero terms; it is not exact at its first $\Z /2$

fig:v10new-ch03-lifts.title: Projectivity supplies a lift $P\to B$ through a surjection $B\to C$. Injectivity supplies an extension $B\to E$ from a submodule $A\subseteq B$. In both pictures the two routes from the upper left to the lower right must agree

fig:varieties.title: Left: the nodal cubic $y^2=x^3+x^2$ in $\R ^2$. Its ideal is prime, so it is irreducible, although it crosses itself at the origin. Right: the zero set of $xz$ and $yz$ in $\R ^3$, the union of the plane $z=0$ and the $z$-axis, two irreducible components of different dimensions

fig:v10new-ch04-multiplicity.title: The ideals $(X)$ and $(X^2)$ both vanish only at $0$. Their quotients remember different relations: $X=0$ in the first, while $X\ne 0$ but $X^2=0$ in the second. Passing to the radical erases that difference

fig:v10new-ch04-staircase.title: For leading ideal $(X^2,XY,Y^2)$, the three surviving monomials are $1,X,Y$. Every marked point outside them is divisible by one of the three leading generators. The survivors will be a basis of the quotient in Exercise~\ref {ex:groebnerhand}

thm:locprimes.title: primes of a ring of fractions

fig:specz.title: After Mumford: the spectrum of $\Z [x]$. The bottom line is $\operatorname {Spec}\Z $. Above each prime $p$ stands the fibre $\operatorname {Spec}\mathbb F_p[x]$, a vertical line made of the generic point $(p)$ and the closed points $(p,f)$, one for each monic irreducible $\bar f$ modulo $p$, of which a few are drawn in grey. The curve is the closure of the point $(x^2+1)$: it meets the fibre at $p$ in two points $(p,x\pm a)$ when $p\equiv 1\pmod 4$, in one point $(p,x^2+1)$ of degree $2$ when $p\equiv 3\pmod 4$, and has its two branches meeting at the single point $(2,x+1)$ of the fibre at $2$, where $x^2+1=(x+1)^2$

fig:v10new-ch05-local.title: Localisation at $(3)$ retains the primes $(0)$ and $(3)$ of $\Z $. Each other $(p)$ meets the denominators, since $p$ becomes a unit, and disappears. Lines show inclusion of primes, not distances between them

fig:v10new-ch05-primary.title: Monomials $x^ay^b$ in $I=(x^2,xy)$ are marked in charcoal. They have $a\ge 2$, or $a\ge 1$ and $b\ge 1$. The rust point $x$ lies in $(x)$ but not in $I$; intersecting with $(x^2,y)$ removes exactly that point from the monomials of $(x)$. The pattern continues upwards and to the right

fig:cubicclass.title: The real points of the cubic $E\colon y^2=x^3-x+1$. The line $y=1-2x$ meets $E$ at $P=(0,1)$, $Q=(1,-1)$ and $R=(3,-5)$, so the ideal it generates in $\C [x,y]/(y^2-x^3+x-1)$ is $\mathfrak m_P\mathfrak m_Q\mathfrak m_R$. The vertical line $x=3$ gives $(x-3)=\mathfrak m_R\mathfrak m_{R'}$ with $R'=(3,5)$. In the class group, $[\mathfrak m_P][\mathfrak m_Q]=[\mathfrak m_{R'}]$: the chord-and-tangent addition of points

fig:v10new-ch06-valuations.title: Valuation coordinates for $I=\mathfrak p^2\mathfrak q$ and $J=\mathfrak p\mathfrak q^3$, with distinct primes. Their sum has coordinates $(1,1)$ and their intersection $(2,3)$. An arrow to the right or upwards means increasing divisibility and decreasing ideal containment

fig:v10new-ch06-splitting.title: The three quadratic patterns in $\Z [i]$: $5$ splits into $(2+i)$ and $(2-i)$ with $(e,f)=(1,1)$ each; $3$ remains prime with $(e,f)=(1,2)$; and $2$ gives $(1+i)^2$ with $(e,f)=(2,1)$. The double mark represents multiplicity, not a second prime. Each column has $\sum ef=2$

fig:surfaces.title: The torus, the Klein bottle and the projective plane, as polygons with edges glued according to the arrows. Each has a cell structure with one $2$-cell, and the boundary of the $2$-cell gives $d_2$: $a+b-a-b=0$, $a+b-a+b=2b$ and $a+a=2a$

fig:v10new-ch07-coefficients.title: Changing coefficients can create a cycle. In degrees $2,1,0$, the projective-plane complex has top differential $2$ over $\Z $ and $0$ over $\Z /2$. The top kernel grows from $0$ to $\Z /2$; the Tor term records the new class

fig:v10new-ch07-cycles.title: A choice of lifts splits $C_n$ into cycles and a copy of the preceding boundary module. The differential is zero on $Z_n$ and maps the chosen copy of $B_{n-1}$ onto its inclusion in $Z_{n-1}$. The decomposition is chosen; the inclusions of cycles and boundaries are canonical

fig:rationalcircle.title: Rational points on the unit circle, from Hilbert's Theorem~90 for $\Q (i)/\Q $: each point $\frac {(m+ni)^2}{m^2+n^2}$ with $1\le m,n\le 7$ coprime is drawn, with the line from $(-1,0)$ of slope $\frac nm$ that finds it

sec:extensions.title: Extensions and the second cohomology group

fig:v10new-ch08-complements.title: Complements for the sign action of $\Z /2$ on $\Z $ are reflections $r\mapsto x-r$. Their mirrors lie at $x/2$. Conjugation by the translation $r\mapsto r+1$ replaces $x$ by $x+2$, so integer mirrors and half-integer mirrors give the two classes in $H^1\cong \Z /2$

fig:v10new-ch08-carry.title: The base-four carry is $c(x,y)=\lfloor (x+y)/4\rfloor $. The rust cells mark pairs that produce one carry. For the triple $(3,2,1)$, the two parenthesisations give carry totals $1+0$ and $0+1$, both equal to $\lfloor 6/4\rfloor $. This equality is the two-cocycle identity

fig:wedderburn.title: Wedderburn's theorem for $\mathfrak S_4$: under the isomorphism of Corollary~\ref {cor:wedderburnCG}, an element of $\C [\mathfrak S_4]$ is a block-diagonal matrix with one block for each irreducible character (Volume~3, Example~11.13), and the $24$ coordinates of $\C [\mathfrak S_4]$ become the $1+1+4+9+9$ free entries of the blocks

fig:v10new-ch09-induction.title: Inducing the trivial representation of a point stabiliser in $\mathfrak S_3$ produces one coordinate for each of three cosets. The average of the coordinates gives the constant part; subtracting it leaves the invariant plane with coordinate sum zero

fig:v10new-ch09-affine.title: The twenty affine maps of $\mathbb F_5$. The four maps with slope $1$ and nonzero translation fix no point; together with the identity they form the kernel of order $5$. Each of the other fifteen maps fixes exactly one point

fig:hooks.title: Left: the diagram of $\lambda =(5,4,2,1)$ with the hook length in each cell; the hook of the cell $(1,2)$ is shaded, of length $6$. By the hook length formula $f^\lambda =12!/(8\cdot 6\cdot 4\cdot 3\cdot 1\cdot 6\cdot 4\cdot 2\cdot 1\cdot 3\cdot 1\cdot 1)=5775$. Right: one run of the hook walk of Theorem~\ref {thm:hook}, from $(1,1)$ to $(3,1)$ (down its leg), then to the corner $(3,2)$ (along its arm). The four corners are marked with dots

thm:hook.title: Hook length formula; Frame, Robinson and Thrall, 1954

fig:v10new-ch10-insertion.title: The insertion and recording tableaux of $31452$. Reverse insertion starts from the cell labelled $5$ in $Q$: remove the $4$ in that cell of $P$, replace the rightmost top-row entry below $4$ (the $2$), and eject $2$. This recovers the last permutation entry

fig:v10new-ch10-hookprob.title: Hook-walk stopping probabilities for shape $(3,1)$. From the top-left cell, three moves are equally likely: two lead to the top-right corner and one to the bottom corner. Averaging over the four equally likely starting cells gives $2/3$ and $1/3$

fig:weights.title: Weight diagrams of two representations of $U(3)$, drawn in the plane $\mu _1+\mu _2+\mu _3=\text {constant}$. Left: $V_{(2,1,0)}$, of dimension $8$: the six permutations of $(2,1,0)$, and the weight $(1,1,1)$ with multiplicity $2$ (the circled centre); restricted to $SU(3)$, this is Gell-Mann's ``eightfold way'' of 1961, in which the eight lightest baryons fill the weights. Right: $V_{(3,0,0)}=\operatorname {Sym}^3\C ^3$, of dimension $10$, whose tenth weight, at a corner of the triangle, was a particle not yet observed; Gell-Mann predicted it in 1962, and the $\Omega ^-$ was found at Brookhaven in 1964

fig:v10new-ch11-growth.title: Adding boxes with at most two rows. There is one path to $(3)$ and two paths to $(2,1)$; the omitted shape $(1,1,1)$ has three rows. For $U(2)$ these multiplicities give the sixth absolute trace moment $1^2+2^2=5$

fig:v10new-ch11-variance.title: Exact power-trace variances for $U(4)$. The values $\min (k,4)$ rise to $4$ and then stay there. Four independent uniform points on the circle instead give variance $4$ at every positive integer frequency. The curves join integer values to guide the eye
